newsitem.title: FRANCE: French 97 borrowing needs estimated at 690 bln Ffr.
newsitem.headline: French 97 borrowing needs estimated at 690 bln Ffr.

text.p: France's medium- and long-term borrowing needs will rise to 689.7 billion francs next year from 528.9 billion this year, a report by the parliamentary finance committee said.
The rise is due partly to the maturity next year of 110 billion francs in "Balladur" bonds issued in 1993, named after former prime minister Edouard Balladur.
It said some 100 billion francs of Balladur bonds, which were orginally meant to be used to buy shares in newly privatised companies on favourable terms, still remained in the market.
A further 15 billion francs would be unblocked through a measure in the 1997 budget allowing people to take out money early from popular savings plans (PEPs).

The report said its estimates for next year's borrowing needs in no way prejudged the government's programme for medium- and long-term borrowing due to be announced by the finance ministry at the start of 1997.

The report noted that the 1997 budget estimated debt service charges at 232.6 billion francs, lower than the 245.1 billion estimated to be required for 1997 in May and compared to 226.4 billion forecast in the 1996 Finance Act.
The reduction compared to the May estimate was due to the recent fall in interest rates, it said.

It said the 1997 budget assumed short-term interest rates of 4.1 percent in 1996 and four percent in 1997. It assumed medium-term interest rates of 5.5 percent in 1997 and long-term interest rates of 6.6 percent in 1996 and 6.8 percent in 1997.
"For 1997, the assumptions used are both cautious and near the market consensus," it said.
